big: Meena wants to buy a ₹1 lakh laptop for her daughter in nine years. She plans to save ₹1 lakh. That plan has a hole in it, and the hole is called inflation.

lines: The laptop costs ₹1 lakh today. I will just save ₹1 lakh over nine years.
Prices rise every year. Let us see what that same laptop is likely to cost when you buy it.

alt: Bars showing the price rising over nine years in lakh of rupees
caps: At 8% a year, it costs about ₹1.26 lakh in three years.
In nine years it costs about ₹2 lakh.
An assumed rate, not a forecast. Goals should be priced in future money.

q: A goal costs ₹5 lakh today. Prices rise about 6% a year. Roughly what will it cost in 12 years?
opts: About ₹10 lakh, since prices roughly double at 6% over 12 years
₹5 lakh, since the cost is fixed once the goal is set
About ₹5.6 lakh, since 6% is added once to the original cost
About ₹15 lakh, since prices triple over any 12-year period
why: At 6% a year, prices roughly double in 12 years, so about ₹10 lakh is a fair estimate.
Prices do not freeze when you set a goal. They keep rising every year.
Growth compounds each year. Adding 6% once understates the rise by a wide margin.
Tripling would need a much higher rate. At 6% a year the rise is about double.

q: Why does automating a SIP or standing instruction help a goal?
opts: It guarantees a profit on every single instalment that you make
Money that moves by itself gets saved; money that waits often does not
It removes the need to review the goal as the years go by at all
It makes the money fully tax-exempt while it sits in the account
why: Automation does not guarantee a profit. It guarantees the habit of saving.
Automation turns saving into a default, so it happens even in busy or tempting months.
Goals still need an annual review, since costs and dates change.
Automation does not change tax. It only moves the money on a set date.

q: Rohan's pay rises 20%, and his spending rises 20% too. Savings stay the same in rupees. What is this called, and what helps?
opts: Market inflation; moving all the money into shares helps a lot
Budget drift; tracking every rupee of spending for a year helps
Savings fatigue; stopping all saving for a month helps a bit
Lifestyle inflation; raising savings with each raise helps
why: Market inflation is about prices. This is about personal spending rising with pay.
Tracking helps awareness, but the term for spending rising with pay is lifestyle inflation.
Stopping for a month does not address the pattern and can weaken the habit.
Spending rises to match income, so savings stay flat. Raising savings with each raise beats it.

q: When should Meena review her goals?
opts: Only when she feels the plan is not working out for her
Every week, so that nothing ever drifts off course
Yearly, and after big changes like a new job, marriage or loan
Never, since a plan set once stays correct for many years
why: Waiting for a feeling lets problems grow. A fixed review date catches them early.
Weekly checks create noise, and markets and costs rarely change that fast.
A yearly review and one after each big change keeps amounts and dates in line with life.
Costs, income and priorities change, so an unreviewed plan drifts out of date.

pts: Price goals in future money, not today's.
Automate saving on the day after your salary arrives.
Review once a year and after any big life change.
